name: Vertical platysma suspension

lead: Vertical platysma suspension is a surgical neck-lift step. The surgeon lifts the platysma, the thin muscle sheet on the front of the neck, and fixes it upward near the ear to tighten loose neck tissue and define the angle between chin and neck.

For looks, the goal is a crisper jawline and cervicomental angle, often discussed alongside facelift, submental fat removal and platysmaplasty. Published reports are surgeon-authored case series and anatomical studies describing results in groups of about 20 to 30 patients.

paras: It is performed by plastic surgeons, often combined with a facelift and removal of fat under the chin. The muscle edge is suspended and anchored to firm tissue near the earlobe. Recovery follows standard neck-lift care directed by the surgeon.

As with other neck-lift surgery, risks include bleeding, scarring, asymmetry and nerve injury; nerve anatomy around the neck is a recurring topic in surgical literature. Candidates are assessed individually by a surgeon.

angle.text: The procedure repositions neck muscle so the underside of the jaw and neck show a cleaner angle, which people seek for a leaner lower face.

lead: Vertical platysma suspension is a surgical technique within neck lifting. The platysma is a thin sheet of muscle across the front of the neck that, with age, thins and loosens and can form vertical bands. Wikipedia lists botulinum toxin and platysmaplasty among treatments for these bands [1].

In a 2006 report in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, surgeons described suspending the free edge of the platysma and fixing it near the earlobe to resistant tissue (Lore's fascia or the tympanoparotid fascia), together with platysmaplasty, in 30 patients, and reported a well-defined anterior neck triangle and long-lasting results [2]. For appearance, the aim is a defined jawline and neck angle.

Other published variants include contralateral midline platysma suspension combined with submental liposuction in facelift surgery [3] and the digastric corset technique with lateral platysma suspension in 20 patients [4].

paras: The platysma runs from fascia over the upper chest and shoulder to the lower jaw and lower face, and contracting it creates a bowstring effect on the neck [1]. Authors of a 2005 review note that submental fat, anterior platysma laxity and relaxed cervical skin all distort the cervicomental angle [3].

The 2006 technique suspends the free platysma edge to Lore's fascia, with a sliding plane between platysma and sternocleidomastoid that avoids the need to undermine the muscle [2]. A contralateral midline approach combines suture-based and muscle-based support [3]. The digastric corset sutures digastric retaining ligaments to the mylohyoid and adds lateral platysma suspension [4]. Anatomical work distinguishes Lore's fascia from the platysma-auricular ligament [5].

Published studies are surgical case series and cadaver work. One analyzed 30 cases and reported satisfactory long-lasting results [2]; another reported results in 20 patients after one year of follow-up [4]; a review of the contralateral technique reported superior postoperative satisfaction [3].
